title: Redwood technical deep dive - OOMs, timeouts, CUDA errors & retry semantics
summary: Deep dive on frequent OOMs and CUDA timeouts in on-prem Dedicated deployment. Covered root-cause hypotheses (batching, KV cache growth, quantization instability, driver mismatches), retry semantics and idempotency, and next steps to collect logs and run targeted repros. Agreed action items and plan for an on-prem POC to run memory-profiling workload.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Claire Huang (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (CTO - Nimbus), Priya Shah (SRE - Nimbus), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng - Nimbus)
Shared links: on-prem POC checklist (link), profiler script (link), benchmark sheet (link)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros? we'll get into the OOMs and timeouts you reported.
[00:12] Tom: Hi, Tom here. We've been seeing repeated OOMs on some high-concurrency routes, especially with long context lengths.
[00:20] Priya: Yeah, and sometimes CUDA driver panics followed by node reboots. It's causing our pod restarts and flapping.
[00:28] Claire: Okay, thanks. We pulled the logs ahead of time, saw some of the cgroup OOM events and CUDA timeouts. First pass — are you on Dedicated or Private?
[00:36] Tom: We're on Dedicated in our colo with your private control-plane; it's basically your Dedicated offering, nodes managed by our infra team.
[00:44] Samir: Got it. Before we dig in, Claire, do you want to run through likely root causes?
[00:50] Claire: Sure. High level: 1) batching + KV cache growth — long conversations can grow KV cache per session and push memory over limits under steady state, 2) quantization artifacts causing unexpected memory patterns (rare but seen), 3) driver/CUDA mismatches or rogue kernels leading to hangs/timeouts, 4) load spikes exposing insufficient OOM kill thresholds or host-level issues.
[01:12] Liam: We're using 8x A100-ish nodes, 80GB. We bumped batch size to improve throughput but then saw OOMs. We tried reducing concurrency and batch size and it helped temporarily.
[01:22] Claire: That matches a classic tradeoff. Which runtime fork are you on? We recently shipped a fix for KV cache eviction in the 1.3 runtime — if you're still on 1.2, you might hit unbounded cache growth for certain streaming patterns.
[01:36] Priya: We're on runtime 1.2.5. We haven't upgraded since it was a big change in infra.
[01:42] Samir: Noted. We'll include upgrade notes in the runbook.
[01:46] [02:00] Claire: Quick note on the KV cache: if you do lots of short requests that start new sessions, we keep KV per pinned session. Long-lived sessions with many prefixes will store a lot. The eviction policy in 1.3 is LRU with size heuristics. In 1.2, sometimes sessions aren't being trimmed correctly.
[02:18] Tom: Is that per-model or per-pod?
[02:20] Claire: Per model instance on the pod. So if you pin the same model across multiple worker processes, each keeps its own KV. That can multiply memory usage.
[02:30] Liam: We saw memory footprint jump linearly with number of concurrent sessions. Could that be duplicated KV caches because of process forking?
[02:38] Claire: Yes. If you launch multiple model workers instead of a single multi-threaded worker, you can get Nx memory. We usually recommend configuring the runtime to reuse KV across workers where possible, or using fewer workers and leveraging batching to improve throughput.
[02:52] Priya: But we were relying on process isolation for fault tolerance. Any downside to switching to fewer workers?
[02:58] Claire: There's a tradeoff: fewer workers may reduce isolation but using our serving runtime's internal concurrency helps you get throughput with lower memory. We can help tune the worker count and batch windows.
[03:10] [05:00] Tom: About the CUDA timeouts — we get the dreaded watchdog message, then the GPU driver resets and the pod restarts. Sometimes there are also 'cuBlas' errors or "kernel not responding" logs. Any immediate fixes?
[03:24] Claire: Often it's either a long blocking kernel (huge batch or very long seq len) or a driver/CUDA mismatch. Check your nvidia-driver version vs the libcudnn/cuBLAS versions we recommend. Also check timeout settings — in some colos the GPU watchdog is aggressive. If a kernel runs > T seconds it gets reset.
[03:44] Liam: We're pinned to driver 525 and cuDNN 8.4. We thought that's compatible with A100.
[03:50] Claire: Usually fine, but some vendor kernels behave differently. We'll share our tested combo in the runbook. Also, quantized kernels sometimes trigger different code paths — especially Q4_0 vs Q8 — which can change execution time and memory access patterns.
[04:04] Priya: I remember one of the errors in the log said something like "CUDA error 59" — our team searched and got mixed guidance.
[04:12] Claire: CUDA error codes vary; 59 is a timeout or driver-specific. We'll ask you to attach the exact nvml/nvidia-smi output and the dmesg. That helps correlate GPU resets to driver logs.
[04:24] Samir: Let's talk retries — when the runtime fails a request due to a transient GPU error, what should the client do? We recommend idempotent retries with jittered exponential backoff. Claire, can you walk retry semantics?
[04:36] Claire: Sure. Our runtime classifies failures by recoverability: transient (GPU reset, transient RPC timeout), fatal (model load failure, incompatible artifact), or soft (response truncated). For transient GPU resets we surface an HTTP 503 with a Retry-After header when possible. Clients should retry but avoid re-sending non-idempotent side-effects; for generation we generally mark them retriable with a token-based idempotency key — that way the backend can detect duplicates if we persist partial state.
[04:58] Tom: We have stateful prompts where token consumption matters. How do we avoid double-charge or duplicate outputs?
[05:06] Claire: For consumption accounting, use the idempotency key and include the original request metadata. We'll dedupe within a short window. If you need strict exactly-once semantics, that's more complex — involves persistent request logs and commit semantics. Most customers use best-effort dedupe plus strong monitoring.
[05:24] Liam: Could retries aggravate OOMs if multiple clients retry simultaneously?
[05:30] Claire: Absolutely — the retry storm is a common pattern. That's why we recommend client backoff plus server-side concurrency shaping, and an optional circuit-breaker that returns 429 when queue depth grows. On Dedicated you can configure backpressure thresholds.
[05:44] Priya: We do see spikes after a batch of retries, yes.
[05:48] Claire: We can help tune your retry policy and add request queue limits per route. Also one fix is to return quick failure for known heavy requests rather than queue them indefinitely.
[06:02] [10:00] Tom: On quantization — we tested int8/4 quantization to reduce memory and it seemed faster in some cases but more flaky in others. Any guidance?
[06:12] Claire: Quantization reduces memory footprint and sometimes increases throughput, but it can change numerical stability. Q4 entailing per-channel scaling vs per-tensor scaling matters. Also: some quantized kernels use custom CUDA kernels that are less mature and may not be well-optimized on all driver versions. We recommended alpha/beta channels before deploying wide.
[06:30] Liam: Do you have a recommended profile per model family?
[06:34] Claire: Yes — in the doc we map families to quant profiles: Llama2-13B -> Q4_0 safe for inference with batch<8; Llama2-70B -> Q5 if you need cost savings but test carefully. We'll attach the mapping.
[06:46] Priya: We tried Q4 on the 70B and had some soft hangs.
[06:50] Claire: That could be a kernel path hitting edge cases — please capture a repro. We'll instrument the kernel call stack.
[06:58] [12:00] Samir: Let's review the logs you uploaded — Claire pulled an excerpt earlier to a shared folder.
[07:08] Claire: Right, excerpt shows repeated pattern: normal traffic spike, one pod shows increasing RSS, then a few CUDA API timeouts, dmesg shows GPU reset, kernel says "GPU hung - resetting", kubelet kills pod, restart. There's also sporadic out-of-memory events at the host level.
[07:26] Priya: The host-level OOM sometimes coincides with other services on the node using swap — we don't have swap in these nodes by design.
[07:34] Claire: No swap means OOM killer is more aggressive. On the other hand swap slows GPU throughput if page faults occur. There's balance. We can recommend node sizing and cgroup limits.
[07:44] Liam: Could NUMA misalignment cause weird memory growth?
[07:48] Claire: Yes — if processes aren't NUMA-aware, memory placement and GPU DMA patterns can cause inefficiencies. We'll ask for numactl bindings and lscpu output.
[07:58] [18:00] Tom: What's your recommended path forward? Upgrade runtime to 1.3, run profiler, test quantization, adjust worker counts?
[08:08] Claire: Correct. Step 1: reproduce with profiler to see where allocations happen (model weights vs KV cache vs temporary activation buffers). Step 2: temporarily reduce worker count and increase batching to see if memory per-concurrency improves. Step 3: test runtime 1.3 in a canary pool — that has KV eviction and some CUDA kernel fixes. Step 4: if driver issues persist, file a vendor support ticket with exact nvidia-smi, kernel, and dmesg traces.
[08:28] Priya: Are there any quick config flags we can change now to reduce immediate risk?
[08:32] Claire: Yes: lower max_batch_size, cap session lifetime to avoid unbounded KV growth, enable early eviction for sessions older than X, set concurrency_shapers per-route, and add circuit-breakers for retries. We can share exact settings.
[08:46] Samir: We'll include an example config for your deployment.
[08:50] [25:00] Liam: Regarding the memory profiler — how intrusive is it? Can we run it in production?
[09:00] Claire: It's lightweight by default — it samples allocation stacks and records peak RSS per request. For heavy duty tracing we recommend running in a mirrored canary or during a low-traffic window; otherwise sampling is safe to run. We can provide a flamegraph output.
[09:14] Priya: We'll schedule a weekend run.
[09:18] Tom: About on-prem POC — what's the timeline and commitment? We want Redwood to run a stress test on our Dedicated cluster to validate fixes.
[09:26] Samir: We typically do a 1-2 week POC for on-prem stacks: week one for instrumentation and profiling, week two for fixes and retest. We'll provide runbook and a list of logs to collect. Pricing for engineering support is in the runbook; I'll attach it after the call.
[09:44] [32:00] Claire: One subtlety: the runtime's retry behavior for generation is to stream partial tokens then finalize — if a mid-stream GPU reset occurs, the partial output might be inconsistent. Our client SDK will either return an error or mark as partial. We can switch to a mode where the server buffers until completion to avoid partial contradictions, but that increases latency.
[10:04] Liam: For us partial outputs are bad; we'd rather fail and retry.
[10:08] Claire: Then set client-side policy to fail-fast on partials and retry with a backoff. We'll set a server-side short window-based dedupe to avoid double-charges.
[10:18] Priya: Are there telemetry hooks for tracing when retries happen so we can watch for retry storms?
[10:22] Claire: Yes — the Console exposes per-request retry counts, queue depth, and token-level latency. We'll enable retention for your account for 30 days for debugging.
[10:32] [40:00] Tom: A few wildcards: what if the root cause is an intermittent kernel bug in the quantized path that only shows under high concurrency?
[10:40] Claire: Then the path is to create a minimal repro that triggers the kernel, capture CUDA stack traces and kernel ids, and work with GPU vendor or open-source kernel maintainers. We'll do one run with the quantized profile and high concurrency to try to trigger it.
[10:56] Liam: Do you need special instrumentation flags to capture the kernel symbol names?
[11:00] Claire: Yes — we may ask for debuginfo or to enable higher nvprof tracing levels for a short run. That produces large data, so do it in a controlled window.
[11:10] Priya: Ok we'll set aside a maintenance window and get you access.
[11:14] Samir: Any legal/security blockers for us to access logs?
[11:18] Tom: We can share logs to a presigned bucket; nothing sensitive. We're fine with Redwood engineers seeing system logs but not PII from app logs.
[11:26] Claire: Great. We'll follow your S3 presigned flow.
[11:30] [55:00] Tom: Quick question on fallback policies — can Redwood automatically fallback to a CPU-serving variant if GPU problems persist?
[11:40] Claire: Yes, we support fallback to a CPU-compatible model variant, but latency will jump. We can configure automatic fallback rules: e.g., after X restarts within Y minutes, switch traffic to a safe variant in another region or to CPU nodes. It's pluggable in the rollout policy.
[11:56] Priya: We'd prefer region fallback before CPU if possible.
[11:58] Claire: You can prefer region fallback; we'll include a sample policy.
[12:02] Samir: To recap action items and next steps: Priya uploads logs, Claire runs profiler, Liam tries to reproduce locally, Samir sends runbook and pricing. We'll aim to reconvene after initial repros.
[12:16] Tom: Sounds good, thanks all.
[12:20] Samir: Thanks, we'll follow up with links and scheduling options.

End of transcript.
notes: Call included AE+SE. Covered upgrade to runtime 1.3, KV eviction, worker count tuning, quantization profile guidance, retry semantics and circuit-breakers, and on-prem POC plan. Agreed to a maintenance window for executions and to exchange logs via presigned S3.
